guides.title: Electricity & Circuits From Scratch
guides.summary: First principles of charge, current, voltage, resistance and power; what a circuit actually is; series vs parallel; reading schematics; using a multimeter; and the physics of electric shock.

sections.heading: Charge and current: the physical basis
sections.body:
Electric charge (symbol Q, unit coulomb, C) is a fundamental property of matter. The elementary charge is e = 1.602x10^-19 C; an electron carries -e, a proton +e. One coulomb is about 6.24x10^18 electrons. Like charges repel, unlike attract, per Coulomb's law:

F = k*q1*q2 / r^2

F = force (N), q1 and q2 = charges (C), r = separation (m), k = 8.988x10^9 N*m^2/C^2.

CURRENT (I, ampere A) is the rate of charge flow past a point: I = dQ/dt, so 1 A = 1 C/s.

In copper each atom donates roughly one valence electron to a shared sea of conduction electrons. An applied field makes this sea drift. Drift velocity is glacial - in a 2 mm^2 copper wire carrying 10 A it is about 0.3 mm/s - yet a lamp lights instantly because the electric FIELD propagates at a large fraction of c = 3.00x10^8 m/s. Analogy: opening a tap on an already-full pipe pushes water out the far end immediately even though each molecule crawls.

Convention trap: CONVENTIONAL CURRENT flows + to -, the direction positive charge would move, because Franklin guessed the sign before the electron was discovered. Electrons physically drift - to +. Every schematic and every diode/transistor arrow uses conventional current. Adopt it and stop thinking about electrons.

sections.heading: Voltage, resistance and power, defined exactly
sections.body:
VOLTAGE (V, volt) is energy per unit charge: V = E/Q, so 1 V = 1 joule per coulomb. It is always a DIFFERENCE between two points - saying 'the voltage at pin 3' silently means 'relative to ground'. Physical analogy: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, resistance is pipe narrowness.

RESISTANCE (R, ohm, symbol capital omega) opposes current. For a uniform conductor:

R = rho * L / A

rho = resistivity (ohm-metres), L = length (m), A = cross-sectional area (m^2). Copper rho = 1.68x10^-8 ohm*m; aluminium 2.65x10^-8; nichrome 1.10x10^-6 (about 65x copper, which is why heating elements are nichrome); glass 10^10 to 10^14.

Metals have a positive temperature coefficient: R(T) = R0 * (1 + alpha*(T - T0)), with alpha for copper = 0.00393 per degree C. A copper winding at 100 C has about 31% more resistance than at 20 C - the reason motor windings draw less current when hot.

POWER (P, watt) is energy per second:

P = V*I = I^2*R = V^2/R

All three forms are the same equation combined with Ohm's law. Energy is E = P*t; the kilowatt-hour is 1000 W for 3600 s = 3.6x10^6 J.

Worked example: a 12 V heater element of 4 ohms draws I = 12/4 = 3 A and dissipates P = 12*3 = 36 W. Run for 20 minutes it consumes 36 W * 1200 s = 43,200 J = 0.012 kWh.

sections.heading: What a circuit is, and the three things it must have
sections.body:
A circuit is a CLOSED CONDUCTIVE LOOP from a source's positive terminal, through a load, back to its negative terminal. Break the loop anywhere and current stops everywhere in that loop - instantly and completely. Every working circuit needs exactly three things:

1. A SOURCE of electromotive force (emf) - battery, generator, solar cell, power supply. Emf is measured in volts and is the 'pump'.
2. A CONDUCTIVE PATH - wire, PCB trace, chassis. Ideally near-zero resistance.
3. A LOAD that converts electrical energy to something else - light, heat, motion, computation.

A fourth practical necessity is PROTECTION: a fuse or breaker sized just above the intended current.

Key distinction beginners get wrong:
- OPEN CIRCUIT = broken path. Current = 0. Full source voltage appears across the break.
- SHORT CIRCUIT = a near-zero-resistance path bypassing the load. Current is limited only by the source's internal resistance and the wiring, so it can be hundreds or thousands of amps. This is how fires and battery explosions start.

GROUND is simply the node chosen as the 0 V reference. In a car it is the metal chassis (so only one wire runs to each lamp). In mains wiring the protective earth is a separate safety conductor, not a normal current path. Mixing up 'signal ground' and 'protective earth' is a classic and dangerous error.

sections.heading: Series and parallel: the two fundamental topologies
sections.body:
SERIES - components share one single current path, connected end to end.
• Current is IDENTICAL through every element: I_total = I1 = I2 = I3.
• Voltages ADD: V_total = V1 + V2 + V3.
• Resistances ADD: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3.
• Failure of any element (a blown bulb) kills the whole string.

PARALLEL - components share the same two nodes, so each has its own current path.
• Voltage is IDENTICAL across every element: V_total = V1 = V2 = V3.
• Currents ADD: I_total = I1 + I2 + I3.
• Conductances add, so 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. For exactly two resistors the shortcut is R_total = (R1*R2)/(R1+R2). For n identical resistors R_total = R/n.
• Parallel resistance is ALWAYS smaller than the smallest branch. If you compute a value larger than any single resistor, you made an arithmetic error.
• One element failing open leaves the rest working - which is why house wiring, car lights and LED panels are parallel.

Worked example - a voltage divider. Two resistors in series, R1 = 6.8 kohm on top and R2 = 3.3 kohm on the bottom, across 9 V. Series total = 10.1 kohm, so I = 9/10100 = 0.891 mA. The voltage across R2 is V_out = 9 * 3300/10100 = 2.94 V. General divider rule: V_out = V_in * R2/(R1+R2). Caution: a divider is a weak source. Connecting a load comparable to R2 pulls the output down - always make the load resistance at least 10x R2, or buffer it with an op-amp.

sections.heading: Reading schematics and measuring with a multimeter
sections.body:
Schematic conventions: a line is an ideal zero-resistance wire; a dot at a crossing means connected, no dot means crossing over. Standard symbols: battery = long/short line pairs; resistor = zigzag (US) or rectangle (IEC); capacitor = two parallel plates (curved plate = negative on polarised types); LED = triangle-and-bar with two arrows pointing away; ground = descending stack of shrinking bars.

Using a digital multimeter (DMM):
• VOLTAGE - measure IN PARALLEL, probes across the component, circuit powered. A voltmeter has very high input impedance (typically 10 Mohm) so it barely disturbs the circuit.
• CURRENT - measure IN SERIES, so you must BREAK the circuit and insert the meter. An ammeter has near-zero resistance.
• RESISTANCE - measure with power OFF and, ideally, the component lifted out of circuit. Parallel paths through the rest of the board will read low and fool you. The meter injects its own small test current, so a live circuit gives nonsense.
• CONTINUITY - the beep function; use it to verify wires, fuses and switches with power off.

The single most common (and most expensive) beginner mistake: leaving the leads in the 10 A current jacks and then probing a voltage source. The meter is then a near-short across your supply - it blows the internal fuse at best, and vaporises the probe tips on a car battery at worst. Habit: after any current measurement, immediately return the red lead to the volts/ohms jack.

sections.heading: Safety: what actually hurts you, and standard practice
sections.body:
CURRENT kills, not voltage - but voltage is what drives current through you. Typical effects of 50/60 Hz AC hand-to-hand:
• 1 mA - threshold of perception, a tingle.
• 5 mA - painful, but you can let go.
• 10-20 mA - 'let-go threshold' exceeded; muscles clamp on the conductor and you cannot release it.
• 30 mA - respiratory paralysis begins. This is why RCD/GFCI breakers trip at 30 mA (or 6 mA in North American bathroom/kitchen outlets).
• 100-200 mA - ventricular fibrillation, usually fatal without defibrillation.

Dry-skin hand-to-hand resistance is roughly 10 kohm to 100 kohm; wet or broken skin can drop to 1 kohm. At 1 kohm, 230 V drives 230 mA - lethal. At 12 V it drives 12 mA - harmless through skin. This is why sub-50 V DC is broadly considered extra-low voltage, but note a 12 V car battery can still deliver 600+ A into a dropped spanner and cause severe burns or a hydrogen explosion.

Standard practice:
• Work on de-energised circuits. Lock out, tag out, then TEST with a meter you have just proved works on a known live source.
• One hand in a pocket when probing anything live - it keeps current from crossing the chest.
• Never work alone on mains.
• Discharge large capacitors (in supplies, microwaves, camera flashes) through a suitable bleeder resistor before touching; they hold lethal charge for minutes to hours after unplugging.
• Size fuses to the WIRE, not the load. Typical copper ampacity: 0.5 mm^2 about 3 A, 1.0 mm^2 about 10 A, 2.5 mm^2 about 20 A in free air.
• Mains work is legally restricted in most jurisdictions. Learn on batteries and low-voltage supplies; hire a licensed electrician for building wiring.

sections.heading: Alternating current, direct current, and why the grid runs on both
sections.body:
Every circuit analyzed so far assumed direct current (DC): charge flows in one direction, driven by a source of fixed polarity, like a battery. But plug a lamp into a wall outlet and something different is happening — the current is alternating (AC), reversing direction back and forth 60 times a second in North America (60 Hz) or 50 times a second across most of the rest of the world (50 Hz). The voltage traces a sine wave: v(t) = Vpeak·sin(ωt), where ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in radians per second. A "120 V" US outlet is not 120 V at every instant — that number is the RMS (root-mean-square) voltage, the DC-equivalent value that would deliver the same average power into a resistor. For a pure sinusoid, RMS = Vpeak/√2 ≈ 0.707·Vpeak, so a 120 V RMS outlet actually swings to about ±170 V peak. This is why a device rated "120 V AC" must tolerate momentary voltages far above 120 — its insulation and components are specified for the peak, not the RMS figure printed on the label.

The choice between AC and DC for the power grid was not inevitable — it was fought over, literally, in the late 1880s in what's remembered as the "War of the Currents." Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station (New York City, 1882) distributed DC at roughly 110 V, and it had a hard physical limit: DC at that voltage could only be economically distributed about a mile from the generating station, because line losses scale as I²R. To deliver a fixed amount of power P at low voltage, you need high current (P = VI, so I = P/V), and resistive loss in the transmission wire grows with the square of that current. George Westinghouse, backing Nikola Tesla's polyphase AC induction motor and, critically, the transformer, offered a way out: a transformer can step AC voltage up for transmission (low current, low I²R loss over miles of wire) and back down to a safe level at the point of use, because a transformer works by electromagnetic induction, which requires a changing magnetic flux — something steady DC cannot provide. No practical way existed in the 1880s to do the equivalent with DC. AC won the grid because of this one asymmetry, and it still runs the grid today, even though modern power electronics has since made long-haul HVDC (high-voltage DC) transmission viable for certain very long runs.

The arithmetic behind that century-old decision is worth doing once, because it explains every high-voltage transmission tower you'll ever see. Suppose a line with 2 Ω of total resistance must deliver 100 kW. At 100 V, the current required is I = P/V = 100,000/100 = 1000 A, and the resistive loss is I²R = 1000²×2 = 2,000,000 W — twenty times the power you're trying to deliver; the scheme is physically impossible, and the line voltage would simply collapse under the load. At 10,000 V (10 kV), the same 100 kW needs only I = 100,000/10,000 = 10 A, and the loss is I²R = 10²×2 = 200 W, just 0.2% of the delivered power. That hundred-fold jump in voltage bought a ten-thousand-fold reduction in loss, because loss depends on the square of current. This is the entire reason transmission lines run at tens or hundreds of kilovolts and step down through substations and pole transformers before reaching your house.

DC hasn't disappeared — it's actually what almost every electronic device wants internally (a phone, laptop, or LED needs a steady DC rail), which is why nearly every AC-powered gadget contains a rectifier (a diode bridge, covered in the components guide) to convert incoming AC back into DC. AC and DC aren't rivals inside a modern device; AC is the transport format, DC is what logic circuits and batteries actually consume.

sections.heading: What "ground" actually means — and why the third prong on a plug matters
sections.body:
"Ground" is one of the most overloaded words in electronics because it means two genuinely different things, and confusing them is a common source of both wiring mistakes and real electrical-shock hazard.

In circuit analysis, ground is just a reference node — an arbitrary point you declare to be 0 V so that every other voltage in the circuit can be stated as "so many volts relative to that point." It doesn't have to be, and often isn't, connected to the earth at all; a 9 V battery circuit sitting on a workbench can have its negative terminal labeled "ground" purely as bookkeeping, with no wire anywhere near actual dirt. This is sometimes called circuit common or signal ground to make clear it's a reference, not a physical connection to the planet.

Mains house wiring uses a second, physically real meaning: earth ground, a wire (usually bare copper or green-insulated) bonded to a metal stake driven into the earth (or building steel or a water pipe) at the electrical service panel. A standard US outlet has three contacts: hot (carries the alternating current from the utility), neutral (the return path, also bonded to earth — but only at the panel, not at the outlet), and ground (the third, round prong), which normally carries no current at all. Its only job is to be electrically connected to the metal chassis of whatever you plug in. Here's why that matters: imagine a fault inside a metal-cased appliance where a frayed hot wire touches the case. Without a ground wire, the case becomes energized at close to full line voltage and simply sits there — silently lethal — until a person touches it and the earth, at which point their body completes the circuit back to the source, and skin/body resistance is easily low enough at 120–240 V to pass a dangerous current. With the case bonded to ground, that same fault instead creates a near-dead-short from hot straight to earth through a very low-resistance path, drawing enough current to trip the circuit breaker or blow the fuse almost immediately — the appliance shuts itself off before anyone touches it. The third prong doesn't power anything; its entire purpose is to make faults fail loud and fast instead of quiet and lethal.

A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI in the US, RCD — residual-current device — elsewhere) is a further refinement required in bathrooms, kitchens, and outdoor outlets. It works by comparing the current flowing out on the hot wire to the current returning on the neutral wire, using a small differential transformer; in a healthy circuit those two currents are identical, since all current that leaves must return through the wiring. If even a small fraction — as little as 4–6 mA in US devices — leaks out some other path, such as through a person's body to earth, the transformer detects the imbalance and trips the circuit within milliseconds, well before the current reaches levels associated with cardiac risk. A GFCI is doing something an ordinary circuit breaker cannot: a breaker only responds to total current through the same wire pair exceeding a large threshold (like 15 or 20 A), which a shock current of tens or a few hundred milliamps through a person never comes close to tripping.

sections.heading: Building Your First Electronics Bench
sections.body: None of this requires a lab — a corner of a desk and a small kit of parts is enough to start verifying, by hand, everything covered above.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (the common "830 tie-point" size is a good first choice; one with a metal backing plate is more rigid), from any electronics/hobby retailer
An assorted resistor kit (values from 10 Ω to 1 MΩ, 1/4 W, ±5% tolerance — often sold as a 300+ piece kit sorted by value)
A digital multimeter (DMM) with DC/AC voltage, resistance, continuity beep, and a diode-test setting — any basic model in the $15–30 range covers this
A pack of jumper wires (a pre-cut solid-core "breadboard wire kit," plus a set of flexible male-male jumpers)
A small assortment of standard 5mm LEDs (red, green, yellow) and a handful of basic silicon signal diodes
A bench power supply, or simply a battery holder set (a 9V clip and a couple of AA holders) as your first DC sources
Safety glasses — cheap, but non-negotiable once you start clipping component leads; clipped leads fly
A small pair of diagonal wire cutters and needle-nose pliers, from any hardware or electronics store
A notebook or spreadsheet to log predicted vs. measured values — the habit that turns tinkering into engineering

sections.heading: Breadboard, Predict, Then Measure: Verify Your First Circuit
sections.body: The single most useful habit in electronics is predicting a number before you measure it, so a mismatch tells you something instead of passing unnoticed.
steps: 1. On paper, sketch a simple loop: a 9 V battery, a 470 Ω resistor, and a red LED (forward voltage Vf ≈ 2.0 V, maximum current ≈ 20 mA) all in series.

2. Calculate the predicted current before touching any hardware: the resistor drops whatever voltage the battery and LED don't, so I = (9 V − 2.0 V) / 470 Ω ≈ 14.9 mA — safely under the LED's 20 mA maximum. Write this number down; you're about to check your own work against reality.

3. With the battery disconnected, build the loop on the breadboard: battery + to one leg of the resistor, the other leg to the LED's anode (longer lead), LED cathode (shorter lead, flat edge on the case) back to battery −.
4. Set the multimeter to DC voltage and connect the battery. Measure the voltage across the resistor alone, then the voltage across the LED alone.

5. Compute the current indirectly from the resistor's measured voltage using Ohm's law: I = V_measured / 470 Ω. Compare this to your 14.9 mA prediction — expect agreement within about ±10%, since a 5%-tolerance resistor and battery sag both introduce small error.

6. Now set the multimeter to its DC current (mA) range, break the loop at one point, and insert the meter in series to read current directly. Confirm it agrees with the value calculated indirectly in step 5 — this cross-check is exactly how you'll catch a wiring mistake or a failed component in real projects later.

7. Add a second 470 Ω resistor in parallel with the first (same two nodes) and re-measure the LED current. It should rise, since total resistance dropped — confirm it against R_parallel = (470×470)/(470+470) = 235 Ω, giving a predicted I ≈ (9−2)/235 ≈ 29.8 mA. At that current a standard LED may exceed its rated maximum and run hot — exactly the failure current-limiting resistors exist to prevent, worth seeing pushed slightly too far on a cheap LED so you respect the limit on everything more expensive afterward.

sections.heading: Beginner misconceptions that quietly wreck your intuition
sections.body:
A handful of mental shortcuts feel true and are not, and they cause more debugging headaches than any single formula gap. The first is "current gets used up going around the circuit" — it doesn't. In a simple series loop, the current is the same at every point, full stop; what gets "used up" is energy, which shows up as a voltage drop across each resistive element, not as a shrinking current. If you measured 15 mA leaving the battery and only 10 mA returning to it, that would mean charge is piling up somewhere in your circuit forever, which violates conservation of charge — it simply cannot happen in a closed DC loop.

The second is "a thicker wire carries a higher voltage," or the idea that voltage flows through wires like water pressure through a pipe and gets used up along the length of the wire itself. In practice, ordinary hookup wire has resistance so close to zero (a meter of 22-gauge copper wire is roughly 0.05 Ω) that the voltage drop along it is negligible next to the drops across your resistors, LEDs, and other loads — essentially all of a circuit's voltage drop happens across its actual components, not its connecting wires. The water analogy for current (charge = water, voltage = pressure, resistance = pipe narrowing) is genuinely useful for building intuition, but it breaks down here: real wire, under normal hobbyist conditions, is not a leaky pipe that loses pressure just from length.

The third, and the one that surprises people most, is about speed. The individual electrons drifting through a copper wire are astonishingly slow — drift velocity in typical hookup wire at modest current is on the order of millimeters per second, slower than a snail. Yet flipping a light switch turns the bulb on instantly. The resolution is that current isn't "electrons sprinting from the switch to the bulb" — it's the electric field established throughout the circuit that starts pushing on every free electron in the wire nearly simultaneously, and that field propagates at a substantial fraction of the speed of light (commonly 50–99% of c, depending on wire geometry and insulation, the same physics behind signal propagation delay in long cables). The electrons that light your lamp were already sitting in the filament before you touched the switch; you didn't send them there, you just told all of them, everywhere in the loop, to start moving together at once.

guides.title: Ohm's & Kirchhoff's Laws With Worked Examples
guides.summary: The three equations that solve nearly every DC circuit - Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's current law and Kirchhoff's voltage law - with full worked solutions, systematic node and mesh analysis, Thevenin equivalents, and the mistakes that produce wrong answers.

sections.heading: Ohm's law: statement, scope and limits
sections.body:
Ohm's law states that for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the voltage across it:

V = I * R,  equivalently  I = V/R  and  R = V/I

V = potential difference across the element (volts), I = current through it (amperes), R = resistance (ohms). The three forms are the same relation rearranged; the memory triangle puts V on top with I and R below.

Critically, Ohm's law is an EMPIRICAL MATERIAL PROPERTY, not a universal law. It holds for metals, carbon and most resistors over their rated range. It FAILS for:
• Diodes and LEDs - current rises exponentially with voltage (Shockley equation), so R is not constant.
• Incandescent lamps - the filament's resistance rises several-fold as it heats; a 60 W bulb measures about 20 ohms cold but behaves as about 240 ohms hot at 120 V.
• Thermistors, varistors, gas discharge tubes, and any semiconductor junction.

For these, use the DYNAMIC resistance r = dV/dI at the operating point rather than V/I, or use the device's actual characteristic curve.

Always combine Ohm's law with the power relations: P = V*I = I^2*R = V^2/R. A resistor sized only by resistance and not by power rating will burn. Example: a 100 ohm resistor across 12 V passes 120 mA and dissipates 1.44 W - a common 0.25 W part will char and drift within seconds; you need a 2 W or larger part.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) - conservation of charge
sections.body:
KCL: the algebraic sum of currents entering any node equals the sum leaving it. Equivalently, sum of all currents into a node = 0, if currents leaving are written as negative.

Sum(I_in) = Sum(I_out)

A NODE is any point where two or more components connect; every point on an unbroken wire is electrically the same node. KCL is simply conservation of charge - charge cannot accumulate at a junction of ideal wires.

Worked example. Three wires meet at node A. Wire 1 carries 5.0 A in. Wire 2 carries 1.8 A in. Wire 3 is unknown. Then I3 = 5.0 + 1.8 = 6.8 A out of the node. If your algebra returns a negative value, that is fine and informative - it simply means the real current flows opposite to the direction you assumed. Never 'fix' the sign by hand; the maths is telling you the direction.

Practical use: KCL is why a parallel branch never 'steals' voltage but does add current draw. Add a fourth LED strip drawing 0.9 A to a rail already carrying 2.4 A and the supply must now provide 3.3 A. It is also the fast way to find a fault - if the current entering a section does not equal the current leaving it, there is a leakage path (moisture, damaged insulation, a shorted component) that is carrying the difference. This is exactly the principle behind an RCD/GFCI: it compares live and neutral current and trips at a 30 mA imbalance because the missing current is going through a person or the earth.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) - conservation of energy
sections.body:
KVL: around any closed loop the algebraic sum of all potential differences is zero.

Sum of voltage rises = Sum of voltage drops,  or  Sum(V) = 0 around the loop

This is conservation of energy: a unit charge carried around a loop and returned to its start must have net zero energy change.

Sign discipline is everything. Adopt one rule and never deviate:
1. Choose a loop direction (clockwise is conventional).
2. Traversing a source from - to + is a RISE (+V). From + to - is a drop (-V).
3. Traversing a resistor WITH your assumed current direction is a DROP (-I*R). Against it is a rise (+I*R).

Worked example - a single loop. A 9 V battery with internal resistance 0.5 ohm drives R1 = 100 ohm and R2 = 220 ohm in series. KVL clockwise:

9 - I*0.5 - I*100 - I*220 = 0
9 = I * 320.5
I = 0.02808 A = 28.08 mA

Check by computing each drop: V(internal) = 0.0141 V, V(R1) = 2.808 V, V(R2) = 6.178 V. Sum = 9.000 V. The sum of drops equals the source - the answer is verified. Always perform this check; it catches nearly every arithmetic slip.

Power check: P_total = 9 * 0.02808 = 0.2527 W. Dissipation in R2 = I^2*R = 0.02808^2 * 220 = 0.1735 W, so a 0.25 W resistor is marginal here and a 0.5 W part is the right choice.

sections.heading: Node-voltage analysis - the systematic method
sections.body:
Node analysis solves any resistive network mechanically. Procedure:
1. Identify all nodes. Pick one as ground (0 V) - choose the one with the most connections.
2. Label the remaining node voltages V1, V2, ... These are your unknowns.
3. Write KCL at each unknown node, expressing every branch current with Ohm's law as (V_this - V_other)/R.
4. Solve the simultaneous equations.

Worked example. A 12 V source connects through R1 = 1 kohm to node A. From node A, R2 = 2 kohm goes to ground, and R3 = 3 kohm also goes to ground. Find V_A.

KCL at A (current in = current out):
(12 - V_A)/1000 = V_A/2000 + V_A/3000

Multiply everything by 6000:
6*(12 - V_A) = 3*V_A + 2*V_A
72 - 6*V_A = 5*V_A
72 = 11*V_A
V_A = 6.545 V

Verify by the divider shortcut: R2 parallel R3 = (2000*3000)/5000 = 1200 ohm. V_A = 12 * 1200/(1000+1200) = 12 * 0.5455 = 6.545 V. Agreement confirms the method.

Branch currents: I(R1) = (12-6.545)/1000 = 5.455 mA; I(R2) = 6.545/2000 = 3.273 mA; I(R3) = 6.545/3000 = 2.182 mA. KCL check: 3.273 + 2.182 = 5.455 mA. Correct.

MESH ANALYSIS is the dual method: assign a circulating current to each independent loop and write KVL for each. Use node analysis when there are fewer nodes than loops, mesh analysis when the reverse.

sections.heading: Thevenin equivalent - collapsing a network to two components
sections.body:
Thevenin's theorem: any linear two-terminal network of sources and resistors is exactly equivalent, as seen from those terminals, to a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistor R_th.

Procedure:
1. V_th = the OPEN-CIRCUIT voltage at the terminals (load removed).
2. R_th = resistance looking back into the terminals with all INDEPENDENT sources deactivated - voltage sources replaced by a short (0 V = wire), current sources by an open (0 A = gap).
3. The load current is then I_load = V_th / (R_th + R_load).

Worked example. A 15 V source feeds R1 = 4.7 kohm to the output node; R2 = 10 kohm runs from that node to ground. Find the output driving a 2.2 kohm load.

V_th (no load) = 15 * 10000/(4700+10000) = 15 * 0.6803 = 10.20 V
R_th = 4.7 k parallel 10 k = (4700*10000)/14700 = 3197 ohm
With the 2.2 kohm load: I = 10.20/(3197+2200) = 1.890 mA
V_out = 1.890 mA * 2200 = 4.16 V

The unloaded 10.20 V collapses to 4.16 V - a 59% sag. This is the quantitative proof of the earlier warning that a resistive divider is a weak source. Rule of thumb: for less than 10% sag, keep R_load at least 10x R_th.

Maximum power transfer follows directly: a load absorbs the most power when R_load = R_th, at which point efficiency is only 50%. That is correct for signal matching (antennas, audio lines) but wrong for power delivery, where you want R_th as small as possible.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and a verification checklist
sections.body:
Errors that produce wrong answers, in order of frequency:
• Mixing units. 4.7 kohm is 4700 ohm; 22 mA is 0.022 A; 100 nF is 1x10^-7 F. Convert everything to base SI units before substituting, then convert back at the end.
• Adding parallel resistors directly. 1/R_total = sum of 1/R. Forgetting the final reciprocal is the single most common slip - people compute 1/R_total and report it as R_total.
• Assuming voltage 'is used up' along a wire. An ideal wire has no drop; both ends are the same node. Real wire does drop: 10 m of 1.0 mm^2 copper (out and back = 20 m) has R = 1.68x10^-8 * 20/1x10^-6 = 0.336 ohm, so at 5 A it wastes 1.68 V and 8.4 W. Always budget wire drop in low-voltage/high-current systems.
• Inconsistent KVL signs - fixed only by adopting one traversal rule and applying it rigidly.
• Ignoring source internal resistance. A tired AA cell can have 1 ohm or more internal resistance; at 500 mA it loses 0.5 V internally, which is why it 'reads 1.5 V' unloaded but the device still fails.
• Sizing resistors by resistance alone and not checking P = I^2*R.

Verification checklist for any solved circuit:
1. Do all node voltages lie between the supply rails? If a node reads above V+ or below ground in a passive circuit, you made an error.
2. Does KCL balance at every node?
3. Does KVL close to zero around at least two independent loops?
4. Does the total power dissipated in resistors equal the total power delivered by sources?
5. Are the numbers physically sane - is any resistor being asked to dissipate more than its rating, or any wire to carry more than its ampacity?

sections.heading: Mesh-current analysis — the loop-based dual of node-voltage
sections.body:
Node-voltage analysis solves a circuit by finding unknown node voltages; mesh-current analysis is its mirror image, solving instead for a fictitious circulating current assigned to each independent loop ("mesh," meaning a loop containing no other loop inside it — a windowpane in a planar circuit diagram). Where node-voltage naturally has one equation per non-reference node, mesh-current has one equation per mesh, and for a circuit with more independent loops than it has nodes, mesh analysis is usually the shorter path to a solution — pick whichever method gives you fewer simultaneous equations.

The method: draw each mesh current (I₁, I₂, …) circulating in the same direction around its window (clockwise is conventional). Any branch shared between two meshes carries the difference of the two mesh currents flowing through it. Then write one KVL equation per mesh, summing voltage rises and drops around that loop exactly as in single-loop KVL, expressing every resistor drop in terms of whichever mesh current(s) actually flow through that branch. Once you solve the resulting system for I₁, I₂, …, every real branch current is recoverable as a sum or difference of the mesh currents that pass through it, and every voltage follows from there via Ohm's law.

Worked example: a two-mesh circuit has, in its left window, a 10 V source in series with a 2 Ω resistor (R₁); its right window has a 5 V source in series with a 3 Ω resistor (R₃); the two windows share a middle branch containing a 4 Ω resistor (R₂), through which the shared current is (I₁ − I₂) when both mesh currents circulate clockwise. Writing KVL clockwise around each loop:

Left mesh: 10 − I₁(2) − (I₁−I₂)(4) = 0 → 6I₁ − 4I₂ = 10
Right mesh: 5 − I₂(3) − (I₂−I₁)(4) = 0 → −4I₁ + 7I₂ = 5

Solving simultaneously (by substitution, or via the determinant method): the system determinant is (6)(7) − (−4)(−4) = 42 − 16 = 26, giving I₁ = [(10)(7) − (−4)(5)] / 26 = 90/26 ≈ 3.46 A and I₂ = [(6)(5) − (−4)(10)] / 26 = 70/26 ≈ 2.69 A. The current through the shared 4 Ω resistor is I₁ − I₂ ≈ 0.77 A, flowing from the left loop into the right loop. This problem didn't resolve to tidy integers, which is normal — real circuits rarely do, and it's exactly why the systematic matrix approach matters more than mental arithmetic once you're past textbook-simple topologies.

sections.heading: Superposition — solving a multi-source circuit one contributor at a time
sections.body:
Superposition is the theorem that lets you split a hard problem — a linear circuit with several independent sources acting at once — into several easy problems, each with only one source active, and then simply add the results. It's valid because resistors, and the KCL/KVL equations built from them, are linear: doubling an input doubles the response, and the response to a sum of inputs equals the sum of the responses to each input alone. It does not apply to circuits containing nonlinear elements like diodes or transistors in their general operating region — only to networks of purely linear components.

The procedure: to find the response due to one source, deactivate every other independent source — replace every other independent voltage source with a short circuit (0 V, a plain wire) and every other independent current source with an open circuit (0 A, removed entirely) — then solve the now-simpler circuit normally. Repeat for each source in turn, then algebraically sum the individual contributions, respecting sign and direction, to get the total.

Worked example: node A is fed by two independent sources in parallel and loaded by a resistor R = 4 Ω to ground. Branch 1 is a 12 V source in series with R₁ = 2 Ω, feeding node A. Branch 2 is an ideal 3 A current source injecting directly into node A. Find the total voltage at node A.

Step 1 — only the 12 V source active (open the 3 A current source, removing that branch): the circuit collapses to a simple series loop of the 12 V source, R₁ = 2 Ω, and R = 4 Ω. Current = 12/(2+4) = 2 A, so this contribution alone produces 2 A × 4 Ω = 8 V at node A.

Step 2 — only the 3 A source active (short the 12 V source, putting R₁ = 2 Ω in parallel with R = 4 Ω, both now running from node A to ground): the 3 A splits by the current-divider rule; the share through R is 3 A × [R₁/(R₁+R)] = 3 × (2/6) = 1 A, giving a contribution of 1 A × 4 Ω = 4 V.

Total voltage at node A = 8 V + 4 V = 12 V, and total current through R = 12/4 = 3 A — which checks against summing the two individual R-currents directly (2 A + 1 A = 3 A). Superposition doesn't just work here; the fact that both routes to the answer agree is exactly the self-check that should become a habit whenever you use it.

sections.heading: Norton equivalents, source transformation, and the maximum-power-transfer trap
sections.body:
Just as any linear two-terminal network can be collapsed to a Thevenin equivalent (a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistance R_th), it can equally be collapsed to a Norton equivalent: a single current source I_N in parallel with the same resistance, now called R_N (R_N = R_th always, since it's the identical resistance seen from the terminals — only the source form differs). The two are related by source transformation: I_N = V_th / R_th, and conversely V_th = I_N × R_N. Being able to flip a stubborn voltage-source-in-series branch into a current-source-in-parallel branch, or back, is often the fastest way to combine two sources that are awkwardly oriented relative to each other, letting you merge them algebraically before doing any real analysis.

A theorem that falls straight out of the Thevenin/Norton framework is maximum power transfer: given a source with fixed Thevenin resistance R_th driving a variable load R_L, the power delivered to the load is maximized when R_L = R_th. This is provable directly from calculus — with I = V_th/(R_th+R_L) and P_L = I²R_L, differentiating with respect to R_L and setting the result to zero yields exactly R_L = R_th — but the number worth remembering is what happens at that maximum: exactly half the total power generated is dissipated in the source's own internal resistance, so efficiency at the point of maximum power transfer is only 50%.

This is where engineers new to the theorem get tripped up: maximum power transfer is not the same goal as maximum efficiency, and for most real power systems you want efficiency, not the theorem's matched condition. Take a source with V_th = 10 V and R_th = 50 Ω (a plausible output impedance for a small audio amplifier or RF source). At the matched load R_L = 50 Ω: I = 10/100 = 0.1 A, delivered power P_L = 0.1²×50 = 0.5 W, and total power drawn is 0.1²×100 = 1 W — efficiency 0.5/1 = 50%, half a watt wasted as heat inside the source for every half watt reaching the load. Now try R_L = 200 Ω: I = 10/250 = 0.04 A, P_L = 0.04²×200 = 0.32 W — less delivered power than the matched case, as expected — but total power is 0.04²×250 = 0.4 W, giving efficiency 0.32/0.4 = 80%. This is exactly why a battery charger, a wall power supply, or a solar charge controller is deliberately designed with the load resistance far higher than the source's internal resistance, not matched to it — chasing efficiency, where matched-impedance thinking would waste half your energy as heat. Impedance matching earns its keep in low-power signal and RF work (audio lines, antenna feeds), where getting the maximum signal through matters more than a wasted fraction of a milliwatt; it's close to the opposite of the right instinct anywhere real power — batteries, mains, motors — is involved.

sections.heading: What You Need to Verify These Laws on a Real Bench
sections.body: The equations above stop being abstract the moment you build the exact circuit they describe and measure it yourself.
ingredients: A digital multimeter (DMM) with DC voltage and DC current (mA) ranges, from any electronics/hobby store
A breadboard and a small assortment of resistors (values like 1 kΩ, 2.2 kΩ, 3.3 kΩ, 4.7 kΩ let you build clean multi-branch networks)
Two independent DC sources — a bench power supply is ideal, or two separate batteries (e.g., a 9V and a 6V pack of four AA cells) with holders
Jumper wires and a set of alligator-clip test leads for tapping into a live circuit without disturbing it
A calculator or spreadsheet set up to solve 2×2 or 3×3 simultaneous equations, by hand substitution or matrix/Cramer's-rule entry, so predictions can be checked quickly
A notebook to record predicted vs. measured values at every node and branch — the discrepancy is often more instructive than the agreement

sections.heading: Verify KCL, KVL and Node-Voltage Predictions on a Real Circuit
sections.body: This turns the whole chapter into something you've personally confirmed with a meter, not just accepted from a page.
steps: 1. Build a simple three-branch network on the breadboard meeting at one node: a 9 V source through R1 = 2.2 kΩ into node A, a second resistor R2 = 3.3 kΩ from node A to ground, and a third resistor R3 = 4.7 kΩ from node A to ground as a parallel load branch.

2. Before connecting power, solve for node A's voltage by hand using the node-voltage method — sum the currents leaving node A through each branch, set the sum to zero, and solve the single resulting equation for V_A. Write down the predicted value.
3. Connect the circuit and measure V_A directly with the DMM's DC voltage range (black probe to ground, red probe to node A).
4. Measure the voltage across each individual resistor and, using Ohm's law with each resistor's known value, back-calculate the current through each of the three branches.

5. Add up the currents flowing into node A and the currents flowing out. They should match to within about 5–10% (the tolerance stack of three 5%-tolerance resistors plus meter accuracy) — your own hands-on confirmation of Kirchhoff's Current Law.

6. Measure voltage drops all the way around one complete loop of the circuit (source, R1, R3, back to source) with the meter, keeping consistent polarity, and sum them algebraically. They should sum to zero, or very close to it — your confirmation of Kirchhoff's Voltage Law.

7. Swap R3 for a different value (say 10 kΩ) and predict the new V_A before measuring again. This rehearses the real workflow: predict, then verify, then trust the prediction on the next circuit you can't as easily probe.

guides.title: Components: Resistors, Capacitors, Diodes & Transistors
guides.summary: What each fundamental electronic component does, the governing equations, how to read markings and choose ratings, canonical circuits (LED driver, RC filter, rectifier, switch, amplifier), and the failure modes that destroy them.

sections.heading: Resistors - values, codes and ratings
sections.body:
A resistor converts electrical energy to heat and sets current or divides voltage. Governed by V = I*R and P = I^2*R.

Standard values follow the E-series, logarithmically spaced so tolerance bands just meet. E12 (10% tolerance) per decade: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. E24 (5%) adds 11, 13, 16, 20, 24, 30, 36, 43, 51, 62, 75, 91. E96 (1%) has 96 values per decade.

Four-band colour code: band1 = first digit, band2 = second digit, band3 = multiplier (power of ten), band4 = tolerance. Colours: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. Tolerance: gold 5%, silver 10%, brown 1%, red 2%. Example - yellow, violet, red, gold = 4, 7, x100 = 4700 ohm = 4.7 kohm, 5%. A five-band resistor has three significant digits then multiplier then tolerance. SMD resistors use numeric codes: '472' = 47 x 10^2 = 4.7 kohm; '4R7' = 4.7 ohm; four-digit '4701' = 470 x 10^1 = 4.7 kohm.

Ratings that matter beyond resistance:
• POWER - typical through-hole: 0.125 W, 0.25 W, 0.5 W, 1 W, 2 W, 5 W. Surface mount: 0402 = 0.063 W, 0603 = 0.1 W, 0805 = 0.125 W, 1206 = 0.25 W. Derate to 50% of rating for reliability and long life.
• VOLTAGE - a 0.25 W through-hole part is typically rated 250 V; exceeding it arcs across the body regardless of power.
• TEMPERATURE COEFFICIENT - metal film about 50-100 ppm/degC, carbon film 200-1500 ppm/degC. For precision references use 25 ppm/degC or better.

Variants: potentiometer (three-terminal adjustable divider), thermistor (NTC drops with heat - used for inrush limiting and temperature sensing), LDR (light dependent), shunt (very low value, e.g. 0.1 ohm, to measure current as a voltage).

sections.heading: Capacitors - charge storage, filtering and timing
sections.body:
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between two plates separated by a dielectric. Capacitance C is measured in farads (F); practical values are microfarads (uF, 10^-6), nanofarads (nF, 10^-9) and picofarads (pF, 10^-12).

Core equations:
Q = C*V   (charge in coulombs)
I = C * dV/dt   (current is proportional to RATE of voltage change)
E = 0.5 * C * V^2   (stored energy in joules)
C = epsilon0 * epsilon_r * A / d   (parallel plate: epsilon0 = 8.854x10^-12 F/m, epsilon_r = relative permittivity, A = plate area m^2, d = separation m)

The defining behaviour: a capacitor BLOCKS DC and PASSES AC. Its reactance falls with frequency:

Xc = 1 / (2*pi*f*C)   (ohms; f in Hz, C in farads)

At 100 Hz a 1 uF capacitor is 1592 ohms; at 100 kHz it is 1.59 ohms.

RC TIME CONSTANT: tau = R*C (seconds). Charging from 0 toward V: v(t) = V*(1 - e^(-t/tau)). After 1 tau it reaches 63.2%, after 3 tau 95%, after 5 tau 99.3% - treat 5 tau as fully charged. Discharge: v(t) = V*e^(-t/tau).

Worked example: 10 kohm with 100 uF gives tau = 10000 * 100x10^-6 = 1.0 s, so a 5 V rail decays to 1.84 V in 1 s and is effectively flat after 5 s.

Types and where they are used:
• Ceramic (C0G/NP0) - tiny, stable, low loss; use for timing and RF. X7R/Y5V are higher capacitance but lose 20-80% of value under DC bias and with temperature - never use Y5V for timing.
• Electrolytic - polarised, 1 uF to 10,000 uF, cheap bulk energy storage. REVERSING POLARITY MAKES THEM VENT OR EXPLODE. The stripe marks the negative terminal.
• Film (polyester/polypropylene) - stable, non-polarised, good for audio and mains snubbing.
• Supercapacitor - farads of capacitance at low voltage (2.7 V typical), for backup power.

Always derate voltage: run an electrolytic at no more than 60-70% of its rated voltage, and prefer 105 degC parts over 85 degC in anything warm - capacitor life roughly halves for each 10 degC rise.

sections.heading: Inductors and the reactive pair
sections.body:
An inductor stores energy in a MAGNETIC field created by current in a coil - the exact dual of a capacitor. Inductance L is in henries (H); practical values are millihenries (mH) and microhenries (uH).

V = L * dI/dt   (voltage is proportional to the RATE of current change)
E = 0.5 * L * I^2   (stored energy, joules)
Xl = 2*pi*f*L   (inductive reactance, ohms - rises with frequency)

An inductor RESISTS CHANGES IN CURRENT, passes DC, blocks high-frequency AC. Interrupting current through an inductor produces a large back-emf spike (V = L*dI/dt with a huge dI/dt) - this is how ignition coils make sparks, and why switching a relay coil or motor without protection destroys the driving transistor. The cure is a FLYBACK DIODE reverse-biased across the coil, giving the collapsing current a path to circulate.

An LC pair resonates where Xl = Xc:

f_resonant = 1 / (2*pi*sqrt(L*C))   (Hz, with L in henries and C in farads)

Worked example: L = 100 uH with C = 100 pF gives f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(1x10^-4 * 1x10^-10)) = 1/(2*pi*1x10^-7) = 1.59 MHz - a typical AM radio tuned circuit.

RC filters, the everyday case. A low-pass RC filter (resistor in series, capacitor to ground) has cutoff:

f_c = 1 / (2*pi*R*C)

At f_c the output is -3 dB (70.7% of input) and it rolls off 20 dB per decade above. Example: R = 1.6 kohm with C = 100 nF gives f_c = 1/(2*pi*1600*1x10^-7) = 995 Hz. Swap the positions (capacitor in series) and you have a high-pass filter with the same cutoff formula.

sections.heading: Diodes - one-way valves and their many jobs
sections.body:
A diode conducts in one direction only. Current flows from ANODE to CATHODE (the banded end); reverse-bias blocks. Behaviour follows the Shockley equation:

I = Is * (e^(V/(n*Vt)) - 1)

Is = saturation current, n = ideality factor (1 to 2), Vt = kT/q = about 25.85 mV at 300 K. In practice, use the FORWARD VOLTAGE DROP approximation:
• Silicon signal/rectifier (1N4148, 1N4007): about 0.7 V
• Schottky (1N5817, BAT54): 0.2-0.4 V, and very fast - use for low-voltage rectification and reverse-polarity protection
• Germanium: about 0.3 V
• LED: 1.8-2.2 V red/yellow, 3.0-3.4 V blue/white/green

Key ratings: I_F (max forward current), V_RRM (peak reverse voltage - exceed it and the diode avalanches), and reverse recovery time (matters above a few kHz).

Canonical uses:
1. RECTIFICATION - converting AC to DC. A full-wave bridge of four diodes gives V_dc(peak) = V_ac(rms)*1.414 - 1.4 V (two diode drops). From a 12 V RMS transformer: 12*1.414 = 16.97, minus 1.4 = 15.6 V peak. A smoothing capacitor then holds this up; ripple is approximately V_ripple = I_load/(f_ripple * C). For 0.5 A load, 100 Hz ripple and 2200 uF: V_ripple = 0.5/(100 * 0.0022) = 2.27 V peak-to-peak.
2. FLYBACK/FREEWHEEL protection across inductive loads.
3. REVERSE POLARITY protection in series with the supply (Schottky, to waste less).
4. ZENER diodes - deliberately operated in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage (3.3 V, 5.1 V, 12 V...) as a simple voltage reference. Always feed a zener through a series resistor: R = (V_in - V_z)/(I_z + I_load), and check the zener's power P = V_z * I_z stays under its rating.

LED WORKED EXAMPLE. Drive a red LED (V_f = 2.0 V, I_f = 20 mA) from 5 V. R = (5 - 2.0)/0.020 = 150 ohm. Nearest E12 value is 150 ohm exactly. Power in the resistor = I^2*R = 0.02^2 * 150 = 0.06 W, so a 0.125 W part is fine. NEVER connect an LED directly across a supply - its exponential curve means a few tenths of a volt extra produces destructive current, and it fails within milliseconds.

sections.heading: Transistors - switching and amplification
sections.body:
A transistor uses a small signal to control a large current. Two families dominate.

BIPOLAR JUNCTION TRANSISTOR (BJT) - current controlled. Three terminals: base (B), collector (C), emitter (E). NPN (e.g. 2N3904, BC547) conducts C to E when the base is about 0.7 V above the emitter; PNP is the mirror image. The defining relation:

I_C = beta * I_B,   and   I_E = I_B + I_C

beta (also called hFE) is current gain, typically 100-300 but varying by 3x between samples of the same part - never design a circuit that depends on an exact beta.

SWITCHING WORKED EXAMPLE. Drive a 12 V relay coil drawing 80 mA using a 2N3904 from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin. To saturate the transistor, drive the base with roughly 10x more current than beta strictly requires (call this the overdrive factor): I_B = I_C/10 = 8 mA. Base resistor R_B = (3.3 - 0.7)/0.008 = 325 ohm; choose 330 ohm. In saturation V_CE(sat) is about 0.2 V, so transistor dissipation = 0.2 * 0.08 = 16 mW - negligible. Add a 1N4001 flyback diode across the coil, cathode to +12 V.

MOSFET - voltage controlled. Terminals gate (G), drain (D), source (S). The gate draws essentially no steady current (it is a capacitor, typically 1-5 nF), so a microcontroller can hold it on for free. Key parameters: V_GS(th) (threshold), R_DS(on) (on resistance, e.g. 0.02 ohm), and gate charge Q_g (sets switching loss). Conduction loss = I^2 * R_DS(on): 5 A through 0.02 ohm = 0.5 W.

Critical selection point: a 'logic level' MOSFET (e.g. IRLZ44N, AO3400) is fully on at V_GS = 4.5 V. A standard MOSFET (IRF540N) needs 10 V and will only partially turn on from a 3.3 V or 5 V pin - it then dissipates enormous power in the linear region and fails. This is the most common MOSFET mistake by far.

AMPLIFICATION - in the ACTIVE region a BJT amplifies. A common-emitter stage with collector resistor Rc and emitter resistor Re has voltage gain approximately Av = -Rc/Re (the minus sign means inversion). With Rc = 4.7 kohm and Re = 470 ohm, Av = -10. Biasing sets the quiescent collector voltage to about half the supply so the signal can swing both ways without clipping.

sections.heading: Choosing, testing and destroying components
sections.body:
SELECTION CHECKLIST for any part:
1. Function and value.
2. Voltage rating with at least 2x margin over the maximum it will ever see, including transients.
3. Current/power rating with 2x margin, then thermal check at your actual ambient temperature.
4. Tolerance appropriate to the job - 5% for pull-ups, 1% or better for dividers feeding an ADC.
5. Package - can you actually solder it, and does it shed heat adequately?

TESTING with a DMM:
• Resistor - ohms range, out of circuit. Reads open = burnt; reads low = a parallel path on the board.
• Capacitor - capacitance range if available; otherwise on ohms an electrolytic shows a rising reading as it charges then goes open. A dead-short reading means it is failed. Bulging or leaking tops mean replace on sight.
• Diode - diode-test mode reads about 0.6 V one way and OL the other. Shorted both ways or open both ways = dead.
• BJT - treat as two diodes back to back from the base. NPN: base-to-collector and base-to-emitter both read about 0.7 V with the red probe on base; both read OL reversed.
• MOSFET - diode-test from source to drain shows the intrinsic body diode in one direction. Gate should read open to both other pins.

HOW COMPONENTS DIE:
• Electrolytic capacitors dry out - their equivalent series resistance (ESR) climbs, ripple rises, and downstream circuits misbehave. They are the number one failure in old power supplies.
• Semiconductors die from heat, overvoltage and electrostatic discharge (ESD). A human can carry 10 kV; MOSFET gates puncture at 20 V. Use a grounded wrist strap and store parts in conductive foam.
• Resistors drift high or open from sustained overpower.
• Reverse-connected electrolytics vent explosively, sometimes within seconds.

SAFETY: high-value capacitors in power supplies retain a lethal charge long after unplugging. Discharge through a resistor of roughly 1 kohm per rated volt (not a screwdriver - that damages the capacitor and throws molten metal), and verify 0 V with a meter before touching.

sections.heading: Integrated circuits and the operational amplifier
sections.body:
Every component covered so far — resistors, capacitors, inductors, diodes, transistors — is a discrete part: one physical device doing one job, wired to its neighbors by hand or by copper trace. An integrated circuit (IC) takes the same building blocks — often dozens to billions of transistors, plus resistors and small capacitors — and fabricates them together on a single piece of silicon, then packages that die with metal pins bringing only the useful nodes out to the world. The leap from discrete to integrated is what took electronics from hand-wired radios to a smartphone: an IC lets a designer treat "amplifier" or "logic gate" as a single component with a datasheet, rather than an assembly of dozens of individually placed parts.

The single most important linear IC to understand is the operational amplifier ("op-amp") — a high-gain differential amplifier IC with two inputs (inverting, marked "−", and non-inverting, marked "+") and one output, sold in simple packages like the classic 8-pin DIP. An op-amp's open-loop gain (output ÷ difference between the two inputs, with no external feedback) is enormous — commonly 100,000 or more — which sounds unusable on its own, since that gain would slam the output to a supply rail for a difference of even a few microvolts, but becomes extraordinarily useful once you add a feedback path: a resistor connecting some of the output back to the inverting input. With negative feedback in place, an op-amp circuit's behavior can be predicted using two "golden rules" that hold for an ideal op-amp: (1) no current flows into either input pin, since the inputs have effectively infinite impedance, and (2) the feedback forces the two input pins to sit at the same voltage as each other, a "virtual short," even though no wire actually connects them.

Those two rules alone derive the most common op-amp circuit without touching the huge open-loop gain number at all. In the inverting amplifier (signal fed through a resistor Rin into the "−" input, feedback resistor Rf from output back to that same "−" input, "+" input grounded), the golden rules force the "−" input to sit at 0 V, matching the grounded "+" input, and since no current can flow into the input pin, all the current arriving through Rin must instead flow onward through Rf, giving the classic result Vout = −(Rf/Rin) × Vin. Worked example: Rin = 1 kΩ, Rf = 10 kΩ, Vin = 0.5 V → Vout = −(10k/1k) × 0.5 = −5 V; the gain is set purely by the ratio of two resistors you chose, not by the op-amp's own enormous and part-to-part variable open-loop gain — which is the entire point of using feedback.

Real op-amps aren't ideal, and the gap matters in practice: the gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is a fixed number for a given part (a common general-purpose op-amp might be rated 1 MHz), and it trades directly against configured gain — set a gain of 100 and usable bandwidth shrinks to roughly GBW/gain ≈ 1,000,000/100 = 10 kHz, above which the amplifier can no longer keep up. Slew rate (volts per microsecond the output can change) limits how fast a large signal can swing regardless of frequency content, and the output can never exceed the supply rails it's powered from — an op-amp running from a single 5 V supply cannot output more than roughly 0 to 5 V, often somewhat less near each rail, no matter what the resistor math predicts.

sections.heading: Reading a datasheet like an engineer
sections.body:
A datasheet is the legal and technical contract for a component, and learning to read one correctly is what separates "it worked on the bench" from "it works reliably in a product." The single most important table on any datasheet is Absolute Maximum Ratings — the hard boundaries (maximum voltage, current, power dissipation, temperature) that must never be exceeded, even momentarily, because doing so can permanently damage or instantly destroy the part; this is explicitly distinct from the nearby Recommended Operating Conditions table, which describes the range the part is designed and guaranteed to perform well within during normal use. A transistor might have an absolute maximum collector-emitter voltage of 40 V but a recommended operating range that keeps well under that with margin — treating the absolute maximum as a target to design toward, rather than a line never to cross, is a common and costly beginner mistake.

Package and pinout information matters just as much as electrical specs. The same silicon die might ship in a through-hole DIP-8 (easy to breadboard and hand-solder), a small-outline SOIC-8 (surface-mount, roughly a third the size), a TO-92 (the small three-legged plastic package common for individual transistors), or a TO-220 (a larger tabbed package used when the part must dissipate real heat, often bolted to a metal heatsink through the tab). Getting the pinout wrong — assuming a part is pinned the same as a similar-looking one from a different manufacturer — is one of the most common causes of "I built it exactly right and it's still dead" failures; always verify pin 1's location and function against the specific datasheet for the specific part number.

Finally, learn to distrust "typical" values and design to the guaranteed worst case. A datasheet often lists a parameter three ways — minimum, typical, and maximum, or for something like transistor current gain hFE, a wide guaranteed range such as 100–300 at a given test current — where the typical number describes a representative unit at 25°C under ideal test conditions, while a real design must work across the full guaranteed range and the part's full rated temperature range, because the units on the shelf will not all measure "typical." Power ratings deserve the same skepticism: a resistor's "1/4 W" rating is usually specified at a stated ambient temperature (commonly 70°C in many datasheets) and comes with a derating curve showing that safe power handling falls as ambient climbs above that point — a resistor happily dissipating 0.25 W on an open bench in a cool room may need to be derated significantly inside a sealed enclosure sitting in direct sun.

sections.heading: Surface-mount vs. through-hole, and why package size isn't cosmetic
sections.body:
Through-hole (THT) components — the kind with wire leads meant to poke through drilled holes in a circuit board and be soldered on the other side — are what beginners almost always start with, because they're forgiving to hand-solder, easy to place on a breadboard with no soldering at all, and physically robust. Surface-mount (SMT/SMD) components instead sit directly on pads on the board's surface with little or no lead length, soldered flat. The industry moved to SMT decades ago for reasons that compound: parts can be packed far more densely, they're placed and soldered by robotic pick-and-place machines rather than human hands at production scale, and — a subtler electrical reason — shorter leads mean lower parasitic inductance, which matters increasingly as signal frequencies climb into the tens or hundreds of megahertz and beyond, where even a few millimeters of extra lead length becomes electrically significant.

SMD passive components (resistors and capacitors) are sold in standardized case sizes named by their dimensions in hundredths of an inch — 0805 (0.08" × 0.05"), 0603, and 0402 are common, running from roughly rice-grain-sized down to barely visible without magnification, with even smaller sizes existing on dense professional boards. For a hobbyist, the practical tradeoff is real but not as forbidding as it looks: 0805 parts are quite manageable with a fine-tip soldering iron, a magnifier, and patience, while smaller sizes genuinely require practice, flux, and often a hot-air rework station or reflow oven to place reliably by hand. This is why through-hole parts remain the standard choice for breadboarding, one-off prototypes, and field repair of older equipment, even though nearly everything manufactured at scale today — including many components sold loose for projects — increasingly ships SMD-only as older through-hole part numbers get discontinued.

sections.heading: Stocking a Basic Components Kit
sections.body: A small, well-organized kit covers the vast majority of first projects and lets you test everything discussed above with your own hands.
ingredients: An assorted through-hole resistor kit (values 10 Ω – 1 MΩ, 1/4 W, 5% tolerance), from any electronics/hobby retailer
An assorted ceramic capacitor kit (small values, pF to a few µF) plus a handful of electrolytic capacitors (1–470 µF, various voltage ratings) — note electrolytics are polarized
A handful of common diodes: general-purpose signal diodes (the 1N4148 family), a couple of general-purpose rectifier diodes (the 1N4001 family), and an assortment of 5mm LEDs in different colors
A few common transistors for practice — an NPN (2N2222/2N3904 family) and a PNP counterpart, both in TO-92 packages, from any electronics store
A cheap general-purpose op-amp IC (single or dual, 8-pin DIP package for breadboard friendliness)
A digital multimeter with resistance, capacitance, and diode-test modes (capacitance mode is a nice-to-have, not essential, on a budget meter)
A breadboard, jumper wires, and a small soldering iron with rosin-core solder for parts you want to keep permanently, plus safety glasses for clipping or soldering leads
A component storage box with labeled compartments — sorting by value the moment you buy parts saves hours later

sections.heading: Identify and Test Unknown Components From a Junk Drawer
sections.body: Reverse-identifying a handful of unmarked parts with nothing but a multimeter is one of the fastest ways to make the earlier sections stick.
steps: 1. Gather a handful of unmarked or unfamiliar parts — pull a few from an old, unplugged broken device (if it contains a CRT or a large capacitor bank, leave those specific parts alone) or from a mixed parts bin.

2. Sort by obvious physical type first: banded cylinders are resistors, small discs or blocks (often blue, brown, or yellow) are ceramic capacitors, cylinders with a stripe and a printed voltage/µF value are electrolytic capacitors, and small three-legged black plastic parts are almost always transistors or voltage regulators.

3. For a resistor, read the color bands, or, faster and more reliable when the bands are faded, set the DMM to resistance mode and measure directly — compare the measured value to what the bands claim as a sanity check on your color-code reading.

4. For a capacitor, check for a polarity marking (a stripe with a "−" symbol, or a longer lead, on electrolytics) before doing anything else with it — reverse-connecting a polarized capacitor in a live circuit can cause it to heat, vent, or fail. If your meter has a capacitance mode, measure it directly; if not, estimate C by charging it through a known resistor (e.g., 100 kΩ) from a known voltage and timing how long it takes to reach roughly 63% of that voltage, reading with the DMM in voltage mode — that elapsed time is one RC time constant, so C = t/R.

5. For a diode, set the DMM to diode-test mode and probe both ways: one direction should show a forward voltage drop (roughly 0.5–0.7 V for silicon, or a visible glow if it's an LED, since diode-test mode supplies a small forward current), and the other direction should show "OL" (no conduction) — this also tells you which lead is which, since forward conduction only happens with the red probe on the anode.

6. For an unknown three-pin transistor, use diode-test mode to probe all six lead-pair combinations. A working BJT behaves like two diodes sharing one common terminal — find the one pin that shows a forward drop to both other pins in one probe direction (that pin is the base), and the polarity of that forward drop (red probe on base for both = likely NPN, black probe on base for both = likely PNP) tells you the transistor type.

7. Log every part's measured value and identity in your notebook or parts box before setting it aside — an unlabeled "junk drawer" component is only useful once, the moment you test it; label it and it's useful for years.

guides.title: Power, Batteries & Solar Systems
guides.summary: Energy and power accounting, battery chemistries and their real capacities, charging discipline, series/parallel pack design, solar panel physics and MPPT, and how to size a complete off-grid system with a full worked example.

sections.heading: Energy, power and the accounting that governs everything
sections.body:
POWER (P, watts) is the rate of energy transfer; ENERGY (E, joules or watt-hours) is power integrated over time.

P = V*I   (watts)
E = P*t   (Wh if t is in hours; 1 Wh = 3600 J; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ)

Battery capacity is quoted in amp-hours (Ah) or milliamp-hours (mAh), which is CHARGE, not energy. To compare across voltages you must convert:

Energy (Wh) = Capacity (Ah) x Nominal voltage (V)

Worked comparison: a 20,000 mAh USB power bank sounds enormous, but its cells are 3.7 V nominal, so it holds 20 x 3.7 = 74 Wh. A phone battery is typically 4000 mAh at 3.85 V = 15.4 Wh. Ignoring losses, that is under 5 charges; after boost-converter and cable losses (typically 15-25%) expect 3.5 to 4.

C-RATE expresses current relative to capacity: 1C discharges the whole pack in one hour. For a 100 Ah battery, 1C = 100 A, 0.5C = 50 A, 0.05C = 5 A. Manufacturers rate lead-acid capacity at the gentle C/20 rate; drawing harder gives you LESS total energy, quantified by Peukert's law:

t = H * (C/(I*H))^k

where H = rated discharge time (typically 20 h), C = rated capacity, I = actual current, and k = Peukert exponent (1.1-1.3 for lead-acid, about 1.05 for lithium). A 100 Ah lead-acid battery at 50 A may deliver only 60-70 Ah of usable charge.

Efficiency multiplies through a chain. A solar system with 90% MPPT efficiency, 92% battery round-trip and 88% inverter efficiency delivers 0.90 x 0.92 x 0.88 = 0.729, or 73% of harvested energy to the load. Always size generation for the END-TO-END number, never the panel rating.

sections.heading: Battery chemistries compared
sections.body:
• LITHIUM IRON PHOSPHATE (LiFePO4). Nominal 3.2 V/cell, charge to 3.65 V, discharge floor 2.5 V. Energy density 90-160 Wh/kg. Cycle life 2000-6000 to 80% capacity. Very flat discharge curve, extremely thermally stable (does not readily enter thermal runaway), tolerates 1C charging. CANNOT be charged below 0 degC without permanent lithium plating damage. The default choice for off-grid storage.
• LITHIUM-ION NMC/LCO (phone, laptop, 18650 cells). Nominal 3.6-3.7 V, charge to 4.2 V, floor 3.0 V. 150-260 Wh/kg - the highest practical density. 300-1000 cycles. Can enter thermal runaway if punctured, overcharged or shorted, venting flammable gas at 150-250 degC.
• LEAD-ACID (flooded, AGM, gel). Nominal 2.0 V/cell, so 12.0 V nominal for six. 30-50 Wh/kg - heavy. Flooded deep-cycle: 500-1200 cycles if you only use 50% depth of discharge; discharging below 50% DoD shortens life dramatically. Cheap, tolerant of abuse, recyclable, and sulfates permanently if left discharged. Flooded types vent hydrogen while charging - ventilate.
• NICKEL-METAL HYDRIDE (NiMH). 1.2 V/cell, 60-120 Wh/kg, 500-1000 cycles, safe, but self-discharges 15-30% per month unless it is a low-self-discharge type (Eneloop and similar hold 70% after a year).
• ALKALINE PRIMARY. 1.5 V, about 100 Wh/kg, non-rechargeable. Excellent 5-10 year shelf life; leaks potassium hydroxide when exhausted and left installed - remove cells from stored equipment.

STATE OF CHARGE by resting voltage (12 V lead-acid, rested 4 hours, no load): 12.7 V = 100%, 12.5 V = 75%, 12.4 V = 50%, 12.2 V = 25%, 11.9 V = discharged. LiFePO4 is nearly useless to gauge this way - its curve sits between 13.0 and 13.4 V for most of the range, which is why those packs need a coulomb-counting battery monitor.

sections.heading: Charging correctly - the discipline that decides pack life
sections.body:
LITHIUM (both LiFePO4 and Li-ion) uses CC/CV: constant current until the cell reaches its target voltage, then constant voltage while current tapers, stopping at about 0.05C (3% to 5% of capacity).
• LiFePO4: CC at 0.2-1C to 3.65 V/cell, hold, terminate at C/20. A 12 V (4-cell) pack charges to 14.6 V and floats at 13.6 V or not at all.
• Li-ion NMC: CC to 4.20 V/cell +/- 0.05 V, then CV. Charging to only 4.10 V costs about 10% capacity but can double cycle life. Never exceed 4.25 V - that is the runaway threshold.
• NEVER charge either chemistry below 0 degC. Discharging cold is acceptable but reduces capacity.

LEAD-ACID uses three stages:
1. BULK - constant current (max 0.2C) until 14.4-14.8 V for a 12 V battery.
2. ABSORPTION - hold that voltage 2-4 hours while current tapers below 0.01C.
3. FLOAT - drop to 13.2-13.8 V indefinitely.
Temperature compensate by -3 mV per cell per degC above 25 degC (about -18 mV/degC for a 12 V battery). An occasional controlled EQUALISE at 15.5 V for 2-3 hours reverses sulfation in flooded batteries - never do this on sealed AGM or gel types.

A BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (BMS) is mandatory for any multi-cell lithium pack. It must provide: per-cell overvoltage cutoff, per-cell undervoltage cutoff, overcurrent and short-circuit protection, temperature cutoff, and CELL BALANCING (bleeding charge from the highest cell so the pack does not become limited by its weakest member). Series cells drift apart over time; without balancing one cell will be overcharged while the pack average looks fine.

Safety notes: never charge a swollen, punctured or water-damaged lithium cell. Charge lithium packs on a non-combustible surface, not unattended overnight when possible. A lithium fire is self-oxidising - a Class D extinguisher, copious water for cooling, or sand; a CO2 extinguisher will not put it out.

sections.heading: Pack design - series, parallel and protection
sections.body:
SERIES raises voltage, capacity unchanged. Four 3.2 V 100 Ah LiFePO4 cells in series (4S) = 12.8 V 100 Ah = 1280 Wh.
PARALLEL raises capacity, voltage unchanged. Four 3.2 V 100 Ah cells in parallel (4P) = 3.2 V 400 Ah = 1280 Wh.
Combinations are written 4S2P, 13S4P and so on.

Why raise voltage? Because for a given power, P = V*I means higher V gives lower I, and losses go as I^2*R. Delivering 1200 W at 12 V needs 100 A; at 48 V it needs 25 A - one quarter the current, one SIXTEENTH the resistive loss in the same cable. This is why serious off-grid systems are 48 V, not 12 V.

Rules for building packs:
• Only combine cells of identical chemistry, capacity, age and manufacturer. Mixing an old cell with new ones makes the old one the limiter and it will be driven into reverse.
• Charge cells to the same voltage (within 0.05 V) BEFORE first paralleling, or large equalising currents flow through the busbars.
• Fuse every parallel string individually, and fuse the pack output within 150 mm of the positive terminal.
• Wire in a balanced topology - take the load from the positive of one end of the parallel bank and the negative from the opposite end, so all cells see equal path resistance.

WIRE SIZING is not optional. Voltage drop:
V_drop = I * (2 * L * rho / A)
with rho(copper) = 1.68x10^-8 ohm*m, L = one-way length (m), A = area (m^2). The factor 2 accounts for the return path.
Worked example: 40 A over 5 m one-way in 16 mm^2 cable. R = 1.68x10^-8 * 10 / 1.6x10^-5 = 0.0105 ohm. V_drop = 40 * 0.0105 = 0.42 V, which is 3.5% of 12 V - acceptable (target under 3% for charging runs, under 5% for loads). Halve the cable to 8 mm^2 and the drop doubles to 0.84 V, wasting 34 W as heat.

sections.heading: Solar panels - physics, ratings and MPPT
sections.body:
A photovoltaic cell is a large silicon diode. Photons with energy above the bandgap (1.12 eV for silicon, corresponding to wavelengths below about 1100 nm) create electron-hole pairs that the junction's built-in field separates, producing current. One silicon cell yields about 0.5-0.6 V regardless of size; CURRENT scales with area and irradiance.

Panels are rated at STANDARD TEST CONDITIONS (STC): 1000 W/m^2 irradiance, 25 degC cell temperature, air mass 1.5. Real-world output is lower. Datasheet parameters:
• P_max - rated watts, e.g. 400 W
• V_oc - open circuit voltage, e.g. 49.5 V (the maximum the panel can ever present)
• I_sc - short circuit current, e.g. 10.4 A
• V_mp / I_mp - voltage and current at the maximum power point, e.g. 41.2 V and 9.71 A
• Temperature coefficient of Pmax, typically -0.35%/degC

TEMPERATURE MATTERS ENORMOUSLY. Cells in full sun sit 20-30 degC above ambient. At 30 degC ambient the cell may be 55 degC, i.e. 30 degC above STC, so power falls by 30 x 0.35 = 10.5%. Conversely V_oc RISES as it gets colder - at -10 degC a 49.5 V panel may reach 56 V, and a string of six would present 336 V to a controller rated 250 V. Always compute worst-case cold V_oc when sizing string length.

MPPT vs PWM controllers. A panel's power curve peaks at V_mp; loading it anywhere else wastes energy. A PWM controller simply clamps the panel to battery voltage - connecting a 41 V-Vmp panel to a 13 V battery throws away roughly two thirds of the available power. An MPPT (maximum power point tracking) controller is a DC-DC converter that continuously hunts for the peak and converts the excess voltage into extra current, typically recovering 20-30% more energy and allowing high-voltage panel strings with thin, cheap wiring. Use MPPT for anything above a trickle charger.

Wiring: panels in SERIES add voltage (currents must match; the weakest shaded panel limits the string). Panels in PARALLEL add current (voltages must match; each string needs its own fuse above 2 strings). Bypass diodes inside the panel let current route around a shaded cell group - which is why shading one cell costs a third of a panel rather than all of it. Orientation: face the equator, tilt roughly equal to your latitude for year-round output, latitude +15 degrees to favour winter.

sections.heading: Sizing a complete off-grid system - full worked example
sections.body:
REQUIREMENT: a cabin with LED lighting 40 W for 5 h, a 12 V fridge averaging 45 W continuous, laptop charging 60 W for 4 h, phone/radio 15 W for 3 h. Location: peak sun hours = 4.2 (a winter-worst figure for a temperate site). Autonomy required: 2 days without sun.

STEP 1 - Daily energy.
Lighting: 40 x 5 = 200 Wh
Fridge: 45 x 24 = 1080 Wh
Laptop: 60 x 4 = 240 Wh
Small devices: 15 x 3 = 45 Wh
Total load = 1565 Wh/day.

STEP 2 - Add system losses. Divide by end-to-end efficiency. With MPPT 0.95, battery round trip 0.95 (LiFePO4), wiring 0.97, and a DC-DC/inverter stage 0.90: 0.95 x 0.95 x 0.97 x 0.90 = 0.788. Required harvest = 1565 / 0.788 = 1986 Wh/day.

STEP 3 - Array size. Array W = 1986 / 4.2 peak sun hours = 473 W. Add 25% derate for dust, ageing, non-ideal angle and temperature: 473 x 1.25 = 591 W. Choose 2 x 400 W panels = 800 W (round up; oversizing is cheap and rescues cloudy days).

STEP 4 - Battery bank. For 2 days autonomy: 1565 x 2 = 3130 Wh. LiFePO4 can be cycled to 80% depth of discharge, so bank = 3130 / 0.80 = 3913 Wh. At 12.8 V that is 3913 / 12.8 = 306 Ah. Choose 2 x 12.8 V 200 Ah in parallel = 400 Ah / 5120 Wh, giving comfortable margin and gentler cycling for longer life. (Had this been lead-acid at 50% DoD, you would need 3130/0.50 = 6260 Wh = 489 Ah - and it would weigh about four times as much.)

STEP 5 - Controller. Array 800 W into a 12.8 V bank: I = 800/12.8 = 62.5 A. Choose an 80 A MPPT controller. Check string voltage: two panels in series at cold V_oc (49.5 x 1.13) = 112 V - fine for a 150 V controller.

STEP 6 - Protection and wiring. Main battery fuse 100 A Class T within 150 mm of the positive terminal. Panel-to-controller in 6 mm^2, controller-to-battery in 25 mm^2 for the 62.5 A run. Check drop on the battery run at 3 m: R = 1.68x10^-8 * 6 / 2.5x10^-5 = 0.0040 ohm; V_drop = 62.5 * 0.0040 = 0.25 V = 2.0%. Acceptable.

COMMON MISTAKES: sizing the array from average annual sun instead of worst-month sun (you run out in December); forgetting the fridge runs 24 h; omitting the DC fuse; using undersized wire and then blaming the panels; mounting panels flat against a roof with no air gap (they run hotter and lose 5-10%); and placing a lead-acid bank in an unventilated sealed box (hydrogen accumulation is an explosion hazard).

sections.heading: Inverters — turning stored DC back into usable AC
sections.body:
Batteries and solar panels are fundamentally DC devices, but most of the world's appliances, motors, and grid infrastructure run on AC — so any off-grid or backup power system eventually needs an inverter to bridge the two. At its core, an inverter synthesizes an alternating output from a DC input using an H-bridge: four electronic switches (typically MOSFETs or IGBTs) arranged so that flipping pairs of them on and off in the right sequence connects the battery's + and − terminals across the load in alternating polarity, producing a voltage that swings positive, then negative, then positive again — the raw shape of an AC waveform.

How closely that shape matches a clean sine wave defines three grades of inverter. A square-wave (or "modified sine wave," more accurately a stepped or quasi-square wave) inverter switches quickly between just a few voltage levels — cheap and rugged, but the resulting waveform is rich in harmonic content far from a true sinusoid, which can cause audible buzzing or humming in transformers and motors, reduced efficiency and extra heating in motor-driven appliances, and outright malfunction or damage in sensitive electronics; some medical equipment, certain variable-speed motor drives, and some audio gear explicitly require true sine input. A pure sine wave ("true sine") inverter instead uses fast pulse-width modulation (PWM) — switching the H-bridge on and off thousands of times per second at a duty cycle that varies smoothly over each half-cycle — followed by an output filter, synthesizing a waveform close enough to a genuine sinusoid to be compatible with essentially everything, at a real cost premium over modified-sine units.

Two numbers on an inverter's spec label deserve more attention than they usually get.
